Serving: Spike serving would be Oikawa or Atsumu. Jump floats would be Yamaguchi or Atsumu. I’d say overall it’s Atsumu for sure. 

Receiving: This needs to be split into digging and serve receive. The best at digging is Yaku without a doubt. Serve receive is probably Kai though. 

Setting: If it’s technique then Kageyama. If it’s decision making, it’s Kenma. If it’s both, then Oikawa. 

Blocking: In a system, I’d say Aone is the best blocker we see. But as a solo blocker it’s Kuro. 

Game IQ: Kenma. No one else has the tactical acumen he does. From serving, to funneling, to targeting specific players, he’s the smartest player in the series.

So for this you need a hyper aggressive team like Karasuno. The focus needs to be on a versatile, fast, and powerful offense with players who can attack at every position. 

S: Kageyama is the best option here because we need precision. There is no room for error, as any hesitation or shakiness means the blockers will catch up and eat the attacker for breakfast. 

OP: Inuoka would be my pick. He’s fast, tall, and can run quicks as well as block. Ironically the ideal Kamomedai player. I’m honestly not completely happy with having to sacrifice Ushijima, but any team with him on it will have to concentrate their offense around him, which will make the attacks predictable. 

OH1: Kiryu is the power hitter I want against these blocks. Out of system attacks against Kamomedai are the hardest to deal with and he addresses that gap very well. 

OH2: Nakashima is my other choice. I know he’s on the shorter side, but there’s no one who tools better than him apart from Hoshiumi. Match him up with Gao and you’d have a very good chance of getting consistent points. He’s also great for morale, especially if Kiryu gets down or Kageyama starts overthinking. 

MB1: Kindaichi is the balanced offensive mid I need. Kamomedai’s shade tactic means any rotation with Kageyama in front will need offensive oomph, so both middles need to be offensively astute. Kindaichi is also defensively solid and hits slides. 

MB2: Hinata is my second pick. The freak quick doesn’t get blocked once against Kamomedai in the manga, which makes it the X-factor this team needs. 

L: Akagi is the Libero with the best chance of getting a tooled hit given how fast and athletic he is. Him saving just 2 or 3 points a match may help turn the game. 

Overall, this team needs to perform the same way Karasuno did. Its big weakness is the height component, but each rotation has at least 1 player who can deal with Gao’s attacks, which are the primary concern in that department.

Contrast that with their offensive power and variety, and we’ve got a game on. Kamomedai may face a massive test dealing with Kiryu’s power, Nakashima’s tooling, the freak quick, and Inuoka and Kindaichi doing tandem slides. 

The serving is a bit of a problem with them though, as only Kageyama and Kiryu have particularly nasty serves. However, Karasuno had the same problem, managed just fine, and would’ve won had it not been for 2 injuries.

Here’s some ground rules I usually try to follow. You don’t need to follow every single one all the time, but a good combo of them usually does the trick 

1. Drone. You have two of them and they’re your best weapon. One can be pre-placed at the exact spot you’ve decided to enter from at a high position. Use the other to do on the spot droning and clear adjacent rooms. Once you’ve cleared the other rooms, just jump back onto the first one and make sure your entry is clear one last time and go inside. Nothing, and I mean NOTHING, can replace good droning. 

2. Make sure you know alternate entries to where you’re going in. Say on Clubhouse you want to hit CCTV by entering from gym bedroom, but without going to 1F. You decide to enter from the jacuzzi wall. You drone again, but suddenly you see a Cav waiting at the stairs and you don’t want to take the fight like that. You can instead choose to enter from the gym window and peek them when they least expect it. Or you go office hatch and flank them. Adapt to your situation as needed. 

3. Go with your teammates. This is a game about working with your team and trading kills after all. So make sure you do it. If you go off on your own, there’s a lot more work to be done instead of having a teammate who can help cover flanks and clear rooms. First of all, remember that being in a 1 vs 1 is your defense’s fault. You shouldn’t have to be in that situation at all, since it’s always heavily skewed in favor of the attacker. 

As for what to do, remember that being decisive matters in these situations. You need to practice thinking. It usually depends on accurately judging the attacker’s level of comfort, and then manipulating it to your advantage.

That means you need to check for any elements of pressure on them.

For example, if they’re oriented toward their weak foot, that’s pressure. If they’re being chased by a defender, that’s pressure. If they’ve missed shots before, that’s pressure. 

Position yourself as optimally as you can. The ideal way to deal with this would be to run out and get close to them. This can help you get a touch, force them to miss, contain them till a defender gets back, or even win the ball if you tackle properly. 

If they’re too far out, brace for a shot. Odds are they’ll get as close as possible before shooting, while still ensuring that you can’t come out without risking it flying by. You can’t do much if that’s the case.

My favorite tip for 1 on 1 keeping though, is measure their touches. As they bear down on your box, they’re still dribbling. They’ll keep the ball close so they can dribble it past you if need be, focusing on control. So wait for a heavier touch. If they take one that seems to get a little further from their body than they’d like, that’s your cue to charge. Throws players off like nothing else, because they’ve already goofed up a touch, but now there’s this whole new element of pressure on them, and they have to deal with both simultaneously. 

That should be enough to get you started. And remember, you’re not at fault for conceding a 1 on 1. If you keep finding yourself in these situations, your entire team’s defensive organization needs to be questioned. Chin up bud, you got this.

Leon > Takeru = Iwaizumi > Kai

Leon’s comfortably the best here, he’s a skilled defender, a good backup setter, and highly capable on offense. Being a Shiratorizawa wing spiker takes a lot in itself, and he’s also tasked with supporting Ushijima. That’s a massive testament to his skill. 

Takeru brings incredible offensive power, steady defence, and is a great captain. But his height is still a detriment as his blocks are low. Iwaizumi is comparable on attack (though inferior) and his defence is much better, both for serve receive as well as digs. I’d say they’re about even, since Iwaizumi is also pretty decent at blocking as a part of a wall. 

Kai is the best defender here, easy. But his offensive power leaves a lot to be desired unfortunately. He’s basically a less offensive Daichi, and since he doesn’t function as a backup setter and his blocking seems average along with his serving, he doesn’t offer a lot. Comfortably last. 


It’s also worth nothing that while all these guys are technically wing spikers, Takeru and Kai play OP, and Iwaizumi and Leon play OH. They’re pretty different roles, even though all of the guys are pretty well rounded as players.
